questions.q: Electric field lines due to static charges
options: start on negative charges and end on positive charges
start and end at neutral points
start on positive charges and end on negative charges
questions.explanation: By convention field lines point away from positive charges and toward negative charges.

questions.q: The SI unit of electric flux is
questions.explanation: Flux = E × area, so its unit is (N/C) × m² = N m²/C (equivalently V m).

questions.q: A long straight wire has a uniform linear charge density of 5 × 10^-6 C/m. Taking 1/(4πε0) = 9 × 10^9 N m²/C², the electric field at a perpendicular distance of 0.9 m is
A thin spherical shell of radius 0.1 m carries a charge of 10 nC. Taking k = 9 × 10^9 N m²/C², the electric field at a point 0.3 m from its centre is
questions.explanation: Outside the shell it acts as a point charge: E = kQ/r² = 9 × 10^9 × 10^-8/0.09 = 1000 N/C.

questions.q: Charges +q and +4q are placed a distance d apart. The point on the line joining them where the net electric field is zero is at a distance from +q of
questions.explanation: kq/x² = 4kq/(d - x)² gives d - x = 2x, so x = d/3.

questions.q: A proton and an alpha particle are placed in the same uniform electric field. Taking the alpha particle's mass as four times the proton's, the ratio of the proton's acceleration to the alpha particle's is
questions.explanation: a = qE/m. Proton: e/m. Alpha: 2e/4m = e/2m. The ratio is 2 : 1.

questions.q: How many electrons must be removed from a neutral body to give it a charge of +1 μC? (e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C)
questions.explanation: Positive charge arises from removing electrons, each carrying 1.6 × 10^-19 C.

questions.q: Using Gauss's law, show that the electric field outside a uniformly charged thin spherical shell is the same as if all its charge were at the centre.
questions.answer: Take a concentric spherical Gaussian surface of radius r greater than the shell radius. By symmetry E is radial and constant on it, so flux = E × 4πr². Gauss's law gives E × 4πr² = Q/ε0, so E = Q/(4πε0 r²), the field of a point charge Q at the centre.
keyPoints: Concentric spherical Gaussian surface and symmetry
E = kQ/r², same as a point charge
questions.explanation: Symmetry lets E be taken out of the flux integral.

questions.q: The electric potential at a point is defined as the
options: work done per unit positive test charge in bringing it from infinity to that point
force per unit charge at that point
total charge stored per unit volume
questions.explanation: V = W/q0 for a slowly moved test charge from infinity.

questions.q: For capacitors connected in series across a battery, the quantity that is the same on each capacitor is
questions.explanation: Charge flowing through a series chain is the same, so each capacitor holds equal charge.

questions.q: The capacitance of an isolated conducting sphere of radius 9 cm in air is (1/4πε0 = 9 × 10^9 N m²/C²)
Point charges of 2 μC and 3 μC are 0.6 m apart in air. Their electrostatic potential energy is (k = 9 × 10^9 N m²/C²)
Four equal charges +q are placed at the corners of a square of side a. The electric potential at the centre of the square is (k = 1/4πε0)
questions.explanation: Each charge is a/√2 from the centre, so V = 4kq/(a/√2) = 4√2 kq/a.

questions.q: A parallel plate capacitor has plate separation 6 mm. A dielectric slab of thickness 4 mm and K = 2 is placed between the plates. The capacitance becomes how many times the air value?
questions.explanation: Effective separation = d - t + t/K = 6 - 4 + 2 = 4 mm, so C' = (6/4)C = 1.5C.

questions.q: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 100 V. Find its kinetic energy in joules and its final speed (e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C, m = 9.1 × 10^-31 kg).
questions.answer: Kinetic energy = 1.6 × 10^-17 J (100 eV); speed ≈ 5.9 × 10^6 m/s.
questions.explanation: The work done by the field equals the kinetic energy gained.

questions.q: Capacitors of 6 μF, 3 μF and 2 μF are connected in series across a 12 V battery. Find the charge on each and the potential difference across each.
questions.answer: Equivalent capacitance 1 μF, charge on each capacitor 12 μC; potential differences 2 V, 4 V and 6 V respectively.
keyPoints: V = Q/C gives 2 V, 4 V, 6 V which add to 12 V
questions.explanation: In series the charge is common and the voltage divides inversely to the capacitance.

questions.q: A material whose resistance decreases as its temperature rises is
questions.explanation: Semiconductors have a negative temperature coefficient because carrier density rises with temperature.

questions.q: The SI unit of electron mobility is
questions.explanation: Mobility is drift speed per unit field: (m/s)/(V/m) = m² V^-1 s^-1.

questions.q: A copper wire 100 m long and of cross-section 1 mm² has resistivity 1.7 × 10^-8 Ω m. Its resistance is
A 1000 W heater is used for 3 hours every day for 30 days. The electrical energy consumed is
questions.explanation: Energy = 1 kW × 3 h × 30 = 90 kWh.

questions.q: Two cells of emf 2 V and 1 V, each of internal resistance 1 Ω, are joined in series with opposing polarities across an external resistor of 3 Ω. The current is
questions.explanation: Net emf = 2 - 1 = 1 V and total resistance = 3 + 1 + 1 = 5 Ω, so I = 0.2 A.

questions.q: A wire of resistance R is cut into four equal parts, and the four parts are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is
questions.explanation: Each part has R/4; four in parallel give (R/4)/4 = R/16.

questions.q: State Kirchhoff's two rules.
questions.answer: Junction rule: the algebraic sum of currents meeting at a junction is zero, which expresses conservation of charge. Loop rule: the algebraic sum of potential differences around any closed loop is zero, which expresses conservation of energy.
keyPoints: Junction rule: sum of currents at a node is zero (charge conservation)
Loop rule: sum of potential changes around a loop is zero (energy conservation)
Used for circuits that cannot be reduced by series and parallel rules
questions.explanation: Both rules are applied with a consistent sign convention.

questions.q: In a meter bridge an unknown resistance X is in the left gap and a 5 Ω resistance is in the right gap. The null point is found at 40 cm from the left end. Find X.
questions.explanation: Resistances of the wire segments are proportional to their lengths.

questions.q: The direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field is given by
questions.explanation: Fleming's left-hand rule relates force, field and current for a conductor.

questions.q: The magnetic field inside a long, tightly wound solenoid is
options: uniform and parallel to its axis
non-uniform and strongest at the ends
questions.explanation: Away from the ends the field inside a long solenoid is nearly uniform and directed along the axis.

questions.q: A wire 2 m long carrying 5 A is placed at 30° to a uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T. The force on it is
A proton circles in a uniform magnetic field. If its kinetic energy is made four times as large, the radius of its path becomes
questions.explanation: r = mv/(qB) is proportional to v. Four times the kinetic energy means twice the speed, so r doubles.

questions.q: In a velocity selector, crossed fields E = 2 × 10^4 V/m and B = 0.1 T are used. Particles passing undeflected have speed
questions.explanation: Undeflected motion needs qE = qvB, so v = E/B = 2 × 10^5 m/s.

questions.q: A wire of fixed length is bent into a circular coil of N turns instead of a single turn and carries the same current. The magnetic field at the centre increases by a factor of
questions.explanation: B = μ0NI/(2R) and R = L/(2πN), so B is proportional to N².

questions.q: Write the expression for the Lorentz force on a charge q moving with velocity v in electric field E and magnetic field B, and state when the magnetic part vanishes.
questions.answer: F = q(E + v × B). The magnetic part qv × B vanishes when v is zero or parallel (or anti-parallel) to B.
keyPoints: Zero if the charge is at rest or moves along B
questions.explanation: The electric force acts on any charge; the magnetic force only on a moving charge.

questions.q: A toroid has 1000 turns and a mean radius of 10 cm and carries a current of 0.5 A. Find the magnetic field inside it (μ0 = 4π × 10^-7 T m/A).
questions.explanation: Inside a toroid B = μ0 n I with n = N/(2πr).

questions.q: The SI unit of magnetic permeability is
questions.explanation: From B = μH, μ has units (T)/(A/m) = T m/A (also H/m).

questions.q: Which of the following is a paramagnetic substance?
questions.explanation: Aluminium is paramagnetic; bismuth, copper and water are diamagnetic.

questions.q: A small bar magnet oscillates in a horizontal magnetic field. If the field strength is made four times as large, the time period of oscillation becomes
questions.explanation: T = 2π√(I/MB), so T is proportional to 1/√B; quadrupling B halves T.

questions.q: At a point on the equatorial line of a bar magnet, the magnetic field is directed
questions.explanation: B_equatorial = -(μ0/4π) M/r³, antiparallel to the dipole moment.

questions.q: A thin bar magnet of magnetic moment M is bent into a semicircular arc. Its new magnetic moment is
questions.explanation: The pole strength is unchanged, but the distance between the poles becomes the diameter 2L/π instead of L, so M' = 2M/π.

questions.q: At a place the vertical component of the Earth's magnetic field is √3 times its horizontal component. The angle of dip is
questions.explanation: tanδ = V/H = √3, so δ = 60°.

questions.q: State Gauss's law for magnetism and state what it implies about magnetic monopoles.
questions.answer: The net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero. This implies that isolated magnetic monopoles do not exist, because magnetic field lines always form closed loops.
keyPoints: Net magnetic flux through a closed surface = 0
Field lines are continuous closed loops
No isolated north or south poles
questions.explanation: Every line entering a closed surface also leaves it.

questions.q: A bar magnet of moment 5 A m² lies at 30° to a uniform field of 0.25 T. Find the work done in rotating it to be perpendicular to the field.
keyPoints: Work done = U_final - U_initial = MB(cos30° - cos90°)
questions.explanation: The potential energy rises from -MB cos30° to zero as the magnet is turned to 90°.

questions.q: Which of the following devices works on the principle of electromagnetic induction?
questions.explanation: A generator produces emf by changing the flux through a rotating coil.

questions.q: A bar magnet is held at rest near a stationary closed coil. The induced current in the coil is
options: dependent on the field strength alone
questions.explanation: There is no change in flux, so no emf is induced.

questions.q: The mutual inductance of two coils is 0.5 H. If the current in one coil falls from 4 A to zero in 0.1 s, the emf induced in the other is
A 20 mH inductor carries a current of 5 A. The energy stored in it is

A conducting rod 0.5 m long moves at 10 m/s in a uniform field of 0.4 T. The velocity makes an angle of 30° with the field, and the rod is perpendicular to the plane containing the velocity and field. The emf induced across the rod is
The north pole of a bar magnet is moved towards a closed circular coil. Viewed from the side of the magnet, the induced current in the coil is
questions.explanation: By Lenz's law the coil face towards the magnet must act like a north pole to repel it, which corresponds to anticlockwise current.

questions.q: State Lenz's law and explain why it is consistent with conservation of energy.
questions.answer: The direction of an induced current is such that it opposes the change in flux that produced it. If it aided the change, the flux would keep growing, producing more current and energy without any work being done, which violates energy conservation.
keyPoints: Induced current opposes the change in flux
Work must be done against the opposing effect
That work appears as electrical energy
questions.explanation: The mechanical work done in moving a magnet is converted into electrical energy.

questions.q: A square coil of side 10 cm with 20 turns and resistance 5 Ω is placed with its plane perpendicular to a field of 0.5 T. The field falls uniformly to zero in 0.2 s. Find the induced emf, the current and the charge that flows.
questions.answer: emf = 0.5 V; current = 0.1 A; charge = 0.02 C.
questions.explanation: The charge also equals NΔΦ/R = 20 × 5 × 10^-3/5 = 0.02 C.

questions.q: The capacitive reactance of a capacitor varies with the frequency of the AC source as
options: proportional to the square of the frequency

questions.q: Resonance occurs in a series LCR circuit when
questions.explanation: At resonance the reactances cancel and the impedance is minimum (= R).

questions.q: The current in an AC circuit is i = 4 sin(200πt) A. Its frequency is
questions.explanation: ω = 200π = 2πf, so f = 100 Hz.

questions.q: A series circuit has R = 8 Ω and impedance 10 Ω and carries 5 A rms. The average power consumed is
An LC circuit has L = 1 mH and C = 10 μF. The frequency of its natural oscillations is closest to
In a series circuit R = 6 Ω, X_L = 10 Ω and X_C = 2 Ω. The power factor is
questions.explanation: Net reactance = 8 Ω, Z = √(36 + 64) = 10 Ω, so cosφ = R/Z = 0.6.

questions.q: Why is electric power transmitted over long distances at high voltage?
questions.answer: For a given power P = VI, a higher voltage means a smaller current. The power lost in the transmission lines is I²R, so a small current greatly reduces the loss. Transformers make it easy to step the voltage up for transmission and down for use.
keyPoints: P = VI: higher V means lower I
AC allows easy voltage change with transformers
questions.explanation: Halving the current cuts the line loss to one quarter.

questions.q: A 200 V rms AC source is connected to a series combination of R = 60 Ω and a capacitor with X_C = 80 Ω. Find the current and the rms voltages across R and across the capacitor.
questions.answer: Current = 2 A; V_R = 120 V; V_C = 160 V.
questions.explanation: The voltages across R and C are 90° out of phase, so they add in quadrature.

questions.q: Which radiation is used in the remote control of a television?
questions.explanation: Remote controls use pulses of infrared radiation.

questions.q: Electromagnetic waves are produced by
questions.explanation: An accelerating charge produces time-varying electric and magnetic fields that propagate as waves.

questions.q: Which of the following lists the radiations in order of increasing wavelength?
options: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light
Visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays
Ultraviolet, X-rays, visible light, gamma rays
questions.explanation: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelengths, followed by X-rays, ultraviolet and then infrared.

questions.q: Sunlight takes about 500 s to reach the Earth. The Earth-Sun distance is about (c = 3 × 10^8 m/s)
An electromagnetic wave in vacuum has electric field amplitude 100 V/m. Its average intensity is (ε0 = 8.85 × 10^-12 C²/N m², c = 3 × 10^8 m/s)
Light of intensity 600 W/m² falls normally on a perfectly absorbing surface. The radiation pressure on it is (c = 3 × 10^8 m/s)
questions.explanation: For total absorption p = I/c = 600/(3 × 10^8) = 2 × 10^-6 Pa.

questions.q: Name one use each of radio waves, microwaves and infrared waves.
questions.answer: Radio waves are used for broadcasting and communication, microwaves for radar and cooking in ovens, and infrared waves for remote controls, thermal imaging and physiotherapy.
keyPoints: Infrared: remote controls or thermal imaging
questions.explanation: Each band is used according to how it is produced, absorbed and detected.

questions.q: Light of wavelength 5000 Å in vacuum enters water of refractive index 4/3. Find its frequency, speed and wavelength in water (c = 3 × 10^8 m/s).
questions.answer: Frequency = 6 × 10^14 Hz (unchanged); speed = 2.25 × 10^8 m/s; wavelength = 3750 Å.
keyPoints: f = c/λ = 3 × 10^8/5 × 10^-7 = 6 × 10^14 Hz and it does not change
questions.explanation: Speed and wavelength both fall by the factor n while frequency stays the same.

questions.q: Which defect of vision is corrected by using a concave lens?
questions.explanation: A myopic eye focuses distant objects in front of the retina; a diverging lens corrects this.

questions.q: White light is dispersed by a glass prism because
options: all colours have the same refractive index in glass
the refractive index of glass differs for different wavelengths
questions.explanation: Different colours bend by different amounts since n depends on wavelength.

questions.q: A double convex lens is made of glass of refractive index 1.5 with both faces of radius of curvature 20 cm. Its focal length in air is
A convex mirror has a focal length of 20 cm. An object is placed 20 cm in front of it. The image is formed
options: 10 cm in front of the mirror
questions.explanation: 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = 1/20 + 1/20 = 1/10, so v = +10 cm: a virtual image behind the mirror.

questions.q: Light passes from glass (refractive index 1.5) into water (refractive index 4/3). The critical angle for total internal reflection at this interface satisfies sin C =
A glass convex lens is immersed in a liquid whose refractive index equals that of the glass. The lens then
options: behaves as a plain glass plate with infinite focal length
questions.explanation: With equal refractive indices there is no refraction at the surfaces, so 1/f = 0.

questions.q: Two thin convex lenses of powers +4 D and +6 D are placed in contact. Find the combined power and focal length.
questions.answer: Power = +10 D; focal length = 0.1 m = 10 cm.
keyPoints: Powers add in contact: P = P1 + P2
questions.explanation: Thin lenses in contact act as a single lens whose power is the sum.

questions.q: A compound microscope has an objective of focal length 2 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm, with a tube length (separation) of 20 cm. Find its magnifying power for the final image at infinity (D = 25 cm).
questions.explanation: Total magnification is the product of objective and eyepiece magnifications.

questions.q: When light passes from air into glass, which of its properties remains unchanged?
questions.explanation: Frequency is fixed by the source; speed and wavelength both decrease in glass.

questions.q: Which of the following can be polarised?
questions.explanation: Only transverse waves can be polarised, and light waves are transverse.

questions.q: In a double slit experiment the fringe width becomes twice as large when
options: the apparatus is placed in water
the distance to the screen is doubled
questions.explanation: β = λD/d is directly proportional to D.

questions.q: Plane polarised light of intensity I0 falls on an analyser whose axis makes 45° with the plane of polarisation. The transmitted intensity is
questions.explanation: By Malus's law I = I0 cos²45° = I0/2.

questions.q: In a double slit experiment light of wavelengths 400 nm and 600 nm is used together. The smallest non-zero path difference at which bright fringes of both wavelengths coincide is
questions.explanation: The common multiple of 400 and 600 is 1200 nm, which is 3λ1 and 2λ2.

questions.q: Two coherent sources have intensities in the ratio 9 : 1. The ratio of maximum to minimum intensity in the interference pattern is
questions.explanation: Amplitudes are in the ratio 3 : 1, so Imax/Imin = (3 + 1)²/(3 - 1)² = 16/4 = 4.

questions.q: What is a wavefront? State Huygens' principle.
questions.answer: A wavefront is a surface on which all points oscillate in the same phase. According to Huygens' principle each point of a wavefront acts as a source of secondary spherical wavelets, and the new wavefront at a later time is the surface tangent to these wavelets.
keyPoints: Wavefront: locus of points in the same phase
Each point is a source of secondary wavelets
New wavefront is the common tangent to the wavelets
questions.explanation: The principle explains reflection, refraction and diffraction.

questions.q: Light of wavelength 600 nm falls on a single slit of width 0.1 mm. Find the angular position of the first minimum and its distance from the centre of a screen 2 m away.
questions.explanation: For small angles sinθ ≈ θ.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: Which observation cannot be explained by the wave theory of light?
options: Emission of photoelectrons with no time delay even at very low intensity
questions.explanation: Wave theory predicts a time lag at low intensity; the photon picture explains instant emission.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: The wave associated with a moving electron is called a
questions.explanation: de Broglie proposed that moving particles have an associated matter wave of wavelength h/p.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: Light of frequency 2f0, where f0 is the threshold frequency, falls on a metal. The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is
questions.explanation: K_max = h(2f0) - hf0 = hf0.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: A photon has energy 3.315 × 10^-19 J. Its frequency is (h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J s)

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: A source emits 6.63 W of monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm, all of it carried by photons. The number of photons emitted per second is (h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J s, c = 3 × 10^8 m/s)

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: Using the relation λ(Å) = 12.27/√V for an electron accelerated through V volts, the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 25 V is

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: Define work function and stopping potential.
questions.answer: The work function is the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of a metal. The stopping potential is the minimum negative potential on the collector that just stops the most energetic photoelectrons, so that eV0 = K_max.
keyPoints: Work function: minimum energy to free an electron from the metal
Stopping potential: retarding potential that makes photocurrent zero
questions.explanation: The stopping potential measures the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: Photoelectrons are emitted with a maximum kinetic energy of 2 eV. Find the stopping potential and the maximum speed of the electrons (m = 9.1 × 10^-31 kg, e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C).
questions.answer: Stopping potential = 2 V; maximum speed ≈ 8.4 × 10^5 m/s.
questions.explanation: Convert the energy to joules before finding the speed.

questions.q: According to Bohr's postulate, the angular momentum of an electron in a stationary orbit is
questions.explanation: L = nh/2π with n = 1, 2, 3, ...

questions.q: The force that holds nucleons together in a nucleus is the
options: strong nuclear force, which has a short range
questions.explanation: The strong nuclear force is attractive and much stronger than electrostatic repulsion, but acts only over a few femtometres.

questions.q: Taking hc = 1240 eV nm, the shortest wavelength in the Lyman series of hydrogen (ionisation from n = 1) is closest to
questions.explanation: The series limit corresponds to 13.6 eV: λ = 1240/13.6 ≈ 91 nm.

questions.q: A sample contains 4 × 10^6 radioactive nuclei with a decay constant of 2 × 10^-3 s^-1. Its activity is
Two deuterium nuclei fuse into helium-4. Given atomic masses: deuterium 2.0141 u and helium-4 4.0026 u, with 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c², the energy released is closest to
In the Bohr model of hydrogen the speed of the electron in the n = 1 orbit compared with the n = 3 orbit is
questions.explanation: v is proportional to 1/n, so v1/v3 = 3.

questions.q: Define half-life and decay constant, and state the relation between them.
questions.answer: Half-life is the time in which half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample decay. The decay constant is the probability per unit time that a nucleus decays (the fractional decay rate). They are related by T½ = 0.693/λ.
keyPoints: Half-life: time for half the nuclei to decay
Decay constant λ: decay probability per unit time
questions.explanation: A large decay constant means a short half-life.

questions.q: Using the Rydberg constant R = 1.097 × 10^7 m^-1, find the wavelength of the first line of the Balmer series of hydrogen (n = 3 to n = 2).
questions.explanation: This is the red H-alpha line.

questions.q: The energy gap of silicon is about
questions.explanation: Silicon has a band gap of about 1.1 eV at room temperature.

questions.q: A p-n junction diode is forward biased when the p-side is connected to the
questions.explanation: Connecting p to positive and n to negative reduces the barrier.

questions.q: An n-type semiconductor is
questions.explanation: The extra electrons are balanced by the positive donor ions, so the crystal is neutral overall.

questions.q: The output of a NAND gate is 0 when
questions.explanation: NAND is AND followed by NOT, so the output is 0 only when both inputs are 1.

questions.q: In a common-emitter transistor amplifier, the phase difference between the output and input voltages is
questions.explanation: An increase in base current raises the collector current and the drop across the load, lowering the output voltage.

questions.q: A photodiode is normally operated in
options: forward bias above the knee voltage
questions.explanation: In reverse bias the small current is easily changed by light intensity, making it a sensitive detector.

questions.q: Explain briefly how a light emitting diode (LED) emits light.
questions.answer: An LED is a forward-biased p-n junction. Electrons from the n-side and holes from the p-side cross the junction and recombine, and the energy released at recombination (approximately the band-gap energy) is emitted as photons.
keyPoints: Electrons and holes recombine near the junction
Energy released is emitted as light
questions.explanation: The band gap of the material determines the colour of light.

questions.q: In a common-emitter transistor circuit β = 100 and the base current is 20 μA. Find the collector current, the emitter current and the current gain α.
questions.answer: Collector current = 2 mA; emitter current = 2.02 mA; α ≈ 0.99.
questions.explanation: The emitter current is the sum of the base and collector currents.
